name: Quill
workload: Call-site latency of LOG_INFO with two ints and a double, 1 thread, async logging to file, percentiles over repeated runs; also backend throughput of 4M messages
claimed_speedup: 1 thread, 90th percentile: Quill 6 ns vs spdlog 296 ns, Boost.Log 3259 ns, g3log 1095 ns; 4M-message throughput 6.44M msg/s vs spdlog 2.57M msg/s
tradeoffs: Unbounded per-thread SPSC queues can grow to 64 MiB each under sustained load (BqLog's benchmark measured multi-GB peak at 10 threads); bounded modes drop messages; needs a backend thread; depends on fmt (bundled).
caveats: Benchmark written by Quill's own author on a heavily tuned machine (isolated cores, mitigations off); tables are in the README, code in a separate repo. Compared with glog only indirectly (glog absent from this table). Latency measures the call site, not time to reach disk.
found_via: Search 'C++ logging library latency benchmark comparison spdlog glog quill NanoLog results'; README performance section
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, Linux RHEL 9.4, isolated cores (isolcpus=1-5, nohz_full, mitigations=off)

name: fmtlog
workload: Call-site latency of a log call with two ints and a double, 1 thread; also own bench with NanoLog message map
claimed_speedup: Quill table, 1 thread: fmtlog 6 ns at 50th/90th percentile vs spdlog 271/296 ns; own README: 6.2-6.4 ns vs spdlog basic_logger_st 156-391 ns (e.g. singleDouble 6.2 ns vs 225.0 ns)
tradeoffs: Drops messages when the queue is full unless FMTLOG_BLOCK=1; requires polling or a poll thread; fmt dependency; per-statement static info table adds binary size (about 50 bytes each).
caveats: Tier A rests on the Quill author's reproducible suite, not fmtlog's own run (own README only says GCC 10.2 tested, no flags). Throughput in Quill's table (2.69M msg/s) is about equal to spdlog (2.57M msg/s); the win is call-site latency. The MuggleWei suite found fmtlog loses logs in drop mode.
found_via: Quill README latency tables; fmtlog README benchmark section
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, Linux RHEL 9.4, isolated cores (isolcpus=1-5, nohz_full, mitigations=off)

name: NanoLog (PlatformLab)
workload: Call-site latency with 1 thread: Quill's table logs two ints and a double; NanoLog README measures six message types vs spdlog v1.1.0, glog v0.3.5, Boost 1.55, Log4j2
claimed_speedup: Quill table, 1 thread, 90th percentile: PlatformLab NanoLog 9 ns vs spdlog 296 ns; own README median latency 7-8 ns vs spdlog 214-1776 ns, glog 1198-2569 ns
tradeoffs: Logs binary; needs a decompressor to read logs; Linux only (macOS partial); preprocessor variant needs a Python step in the build; blocks when its buffer is full.
caveats: Tier A rests on the Quill suite; the README's own numbers use old versions (spdlog v1.1.0, glog v0.3.5) and no stated CPU or flags. The MuggleWei suite lists it among the fastest with no log loss.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, Linux RHEL 9.4, isolated cores (isolcpus=1-5, nohz_full, mitigations=off)

name: XTR
workload: Call-site latency with two ints and a double, 1 thread; throughput of 4M messages
claimed_speedup: Quill table, 1 thread, 90th percentile: XTR 6 ns vs spdlog 296 ns; throughput 7.73M msg/s vs spdlog 2.57M msg/s; own README 0.9-1.3 ns per call on Ryzen 5950X
tradeoffs: Needs fmt; no allocations on the log path; optional io_uring backend; fewer formatting features than spdlog.
caveats: Tier A rests on the Quill suite (run by a competitor). XTR's own README gives numbers only for itself, no spdlog comparison; its own call-site numbers (about 1 ns) measure enqueue only.
found_via: Quill README latency and throughput tables
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, Linux RHEL 9.4, isolated cores (isolcpus=1-5, nohz_full, mitigations=off)

name: binlog (Morgan Stanley)
workload: Call-site latency with two ints and a double, 1 thread; structured binary logs
claimed_speedup: Quill table, 1 thread, 90th percentile: MS BinLog 18 ns vs spdlog 296 ns; vector-of-strings case 64 ns vs spdlog 7120 ns
tradeoffs: Binary log format needs bread to read; archived on GitHub (read-only since 2026-07-01); no text output on the hot path.
caveats: Tier A rests on the Quill suite; binlog's own README numbers (Xeon E5-2698) do not compare against spdlog. Archived, so no further fixes.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, Linux RHEL 9.4, isolated cores (isolcpus=1-5, nohz_full, mitigations=off)

name: BqLog
workload: 1-10 threads each writing 2,000,000 four-parameter log entries to disk, total time until flushed (spdlog async, glog sync, fmtlog, quill, Log4j2)
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: BqLog compressed 95 ms vs spdlog async 560 ms, glog 4485 ms, quill 639 ms, fmtlog 672 ms; 10 threads: 507 ms vs spdlog 32939 ms, glog 127550 ms; BqLog text mode 258 ms at 1 thread; README says 6-65x faster than spdlog async, 47-252x than glog
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 14.51 Release x64 (runnable project at tag benchmark_2.5.0; spdlog 1.17.0, glog 0.7.1, quill 11.1.0)
stars_or_usage: 645 stars; used in Honor of Kings
tradeoffs: Fastest mode writes a compressed binary format; text mode is slower; multi-language API.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the project, Windows/MSVC only and flags given only as Release (hence tier C). Spdlog configured with an 8192-slot blocking queue; glog is synchronous so its row compares unlike designs. In Quill's latency suite BqLog's call-site latency is 138 ns at 90th percentile, slower than Quill and fmtlog.
found_via: Quill README tables list BqLog; opened its docs/BENCHMARK.md

name: NanoLog (Iyengar111)
workload: Call-site latency over 1-5 threads, guaranteed (no loss) and non-guaranteed ring-buffer variants, vs spdlog, g3log, reckless
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: guaranteed logger averages 0.35 microseconds vs spdlog 2.59 microseconds; non-guaranteed averages 131 ns; Quill table 1 thread 90th percentile 155 ns vs spdlog 296 ns
tradeoffs: Single-header C++11 logger; text output; the weakest of the fast loggers in Quill's table (about 3x slower than PlatformLab NanoLog at 1 thread).
caveats: Old spdlog version and 2015-era hardware; own numbers, no build flags stated; no license file found at LICENSE or LICENSE.txt on the default branch, so treated as reference. Different project from PlatformLab/NanoLog.
found_via: Quill README tables list Iyengar NanoLog; opened its README

name: haclog
workload: Google Benchmark of writing a struct message (u64, u32, i64, i32, 128-byte string) to a file, 1-8 threads and hardware-concurrency multiples; nine C/C++ loggers
claimed_speedup: Chart-only (SVG): haclog listed among the fastest in the non-stress scenario with fmtlog, Nanolog and quill; slows markedly once its buffer fills
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.1, Google Benchmark 1.8.3 (other flags not stated)
hardware: Intel i7-10710U laptop, CPU frequency pinned to 3.2 GHz, Arch Linux 6.11.9
tradeoffs: Plain C API; blocks when the buffer is full (no loss); throughput drops when the buffer saturates.
caveats: The comparison suite is run by haclog's own author, and its numbers are in SVG charts only, so no figure could be quoted from the page (tier C). Suite also includes glog, spdlog, reckless, loguru, easylogging++ and found them slower than the async group. Opened README of cc_log_benchmark; haclog repo page showed no numbers.
found_via: Search results for cc_log_benchmark; opened MuggleWei/cc_log_benchmark README

name: fastrace
workload: Creating and reporting spans, 1 to 1000 spans per trace, on four CPU architectures
claimed_speedup: 100 spans: tokio-tracing 124x slower and rustracing 45x slower than fastrace (3.4 us) on Intel Broadwell; 1000 spans: tokio-tracing 151x slower (fastrace 27.8 us); 1 span: tokio-tracing 19x slower
hardware: Intel Broadwell, Skylake, AMD Zen, AWS Graviton2 (models not further specified)
tradeoffs: Rust crate (not usable from C++); exports to OpenTelemetry through fastrace-opentelemetry; different API from tokio-tracing.
caveats: Compared against tokio-tracing and rustracing, not against the OpenTelemetry SDK itself, so baseline_in_list is false. Benchmark setup (compiler flags, exact CPUs) not stated on the README; detailed results live in benches/results which I did not open.
found_via: Search 'fastrace Rust tracing library faster than OpenTelemetry benchmark'
